summary: A 1977 specification of a remote job entry protocol for a resource sharing network, prepared for the Defense Communications Agency. Remote job entry means submitting batch work to a remote computer and getting results back.

eli5.summary: You hand in a stack of work to a far-away computer and later get the results. This note describes the rules for doing that.

questions: how do you submit jobs to remote computers
subtitle: A flexible protocol for submitting batch jobs to remote computers over a network.

tldr.problem: The existing NETRJE protocol required large implementation effort and created security vulnerabilities, particularly around storing passwords for unattended output delivery ("hot line printer").
tldr.mechanism: RFC 725 proposes a simpler RJE protocol with three levels of implementation: Telnet-only (minimal), Telnet with dedicated data transfer (better performance), and FTP-based (convenient for file-system access). All three levels coexist, letting sites implement only what they need.
tldr.outcome: The approach reduced implementation burden and eliminated the need to store remote passwords. The protocol also introduced performance measurement capabilities to track job costs and protocol efficiency.

today: RFC 725 is a proposal for RJE over ARPANET, now Historic. Modern batch job submission uses SSH, HTTP-based job scheduling systems, or cloud provider APIs, but the protocol's principle of offering multiple implementation levels remains relevant in infrastructure design.

sections.title: Why a New RJE Protocol
sections.content: RFC 725 addresses limitations of the existing NETRJE protocol used on the ARPANET. The old protocol required implementers to support Telnet, FTP, and RJE simultaneously, creating a heavy burden on user sites that just wanted basic job submission. More seriously, it required storing user passwords and credentials at remote sites to support automated output printing ("hot line printer"), creating significant security risks. The new protocol solves these problems by offering multiple implementation levels and requiring users, not servers, to manage automated output delivery.
sections.eli5: The old way was complicated and unsafe. This new way lets you choose how fancy to get, and doesn't make servers store your passwords.

sections.title: Three Levels of Service
sections.content: RFC 725 defines three models that coexist and work together. The Telnet-only model is the simplest: all job control, data, and replies travel over a single Telnet connection, useful for minimal implementations or systems with tight resource constraints. The Telnet with Data Transfer model uses a separate data connection for job input and output while keeping control on Telnet, improving efficiency without requiring a full FTP implementation. The FTP model lets users transfer job input and output through FTP, convenient for sites that already run FTP and prefer operating on files in the local file system. Servers should support at least the simpler models, and all three can interoperate transparently based on what each party prefers.
sections.eli5: You can use the simple way (everything on one channel), the better way (separate data channel), or the fancy way (use files). Pick what works for you.

sections.title: Job Submission and Retrieval
sections.content: The protocol defines commands for the full RJE cycle. SCHED submits a job and specifies where output should go. INPATH and OUTPATH (for FTP model) return pathnames at the server where input can be placed or output retrieved. OUTPUT retrieves completed job output and can direct it to a specific host, socket, or the Telnet connection. STATUS checks the status of jobs or RJE sessions. INDEF and OUTDEF configure input and output parameters without immediately transferring data. The protocol follows FTP's reply code structure for consistency, and includes commands like CANCEL, ABORT, and MEASURE for job control and performance metrics.
sections.eli5: Send commands to submit jobs, check on them, get results back, and see how long they took.
